title: Faith that moves mountains (Mark 11:20–25)
hookLine: have faith in God, and when you pray, forgive
last: A HOUSE OF PRAYER FOR ALL.

cards: A dead tree by the roadside, the morning after. Walking in from Bethany again, they pass yesterday's fig tree, dried up from the roots. Peter remembers, and points, a little stunned.
In the King James Bible: "Master, behold, the fig tree which thou cursedst is withered away." You can hear him wanting an explanation. What was that about?
And Jesus doesn't talk about fig trees at all, or explain the temple. He talks about prayer, and about a mountain.
Then, where you'd expect something grand, he ends somewhere very small, as close as the people you live with.

teach.b: Jesus begins with four words: "Have faith in God."

Then the big picture: whoever says to this mountain, be lifted up and thrown into the sea, and doesn't doubt in their heart, it will happen. They're walking near the Mount of Olives, within sight of the temple mount.
Moving a mountain was a way of saying doing the impossible; later Jewish teachers praised a brilliant rabbi as an uprooter of mountains.
Then he goes further: whatever you ask for in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours. Some Christians hear a bold promise to pray big.
Others warn against treating it like a vending machine, and read it next to places where Jesus prays that God's will be done.
Some hold the two together: pray boldly, and trust.
But look at the very next sentence: "And when ye stand praying, forgive, if ye have ought against any: that your Father also which is in heaven may forgive you your trespasses."
Right after the mountain, the condition isn't more faith. It's forgiveness. In Mark, the letting go comes before the asking.

teach.h: WHEN YE STAND PRAYING, FORGIVE, IF YE HAVE OUGHT AGAINST ANY.
teach.b: The Greek word for forgive here, aphiēmi, also means to release, like opening your hand and dropping something. Mark uses the same verb in chapter one, when the fishermen leave their nets.
The fig tree without fruit, the temple without prayer, and now this: some readers hear one lesson in all three, that the fruit Jesus looks for starts close to home, with a grudge put down.

how: Some Christians make a habit of forgiving others before they pray, and in some churches people exchange a sign of peace before communion, echoing Jesus's words that forgiveness comes before prayer.

o: to pray boldly for the impossible
to have faith that never doubts
to release, to let go of, to forgive

games.q: what's inside the passage — tap the pairs.

s: Jesus explains what the fig tree meant
he doesn't; he talks about faith, prayer and forgiveness.
the promise about mountains ends with forgiveness
moving mountains was a way of saying doing the impossible
later Jewish teachers called a great rabbi an uprooter of mountains.

games.q: you've just heard that faith can move a mountain. what's the very next thing Jesus says to do when you pray?
o: forgive anyone you hold something against.
games.why: "when ye stand praying, forgive, if ye have ought against any." the mountain, then the grudge.

practice: Is there someone you have ought against, as the old English says, big or small?
Let their face come to mind; you don't have to feel warm, pretend it didn't matter, or call them, just picture opening your hand and letting the grudge drop, even for these two minutes.
If you pray, do that first and then bring your prayer; if you don't, notice what your hand feels like, open.

wordCard.voice: Aphiemi, the Greek word for forgive, to let go, to release. Pray boldly, trust God, and before you ask, forgive.

orig.note: Greek: forgive, let go, release. from aphiēmi, also used for leaving nets behind.

carryVoice: Your line: forgive, then pray. The letting go comes first. That's day two hundred eight.
